title: Observability
subtitle: Use metrics, logs, and traces to detect impact and locate causes
objectives: Distinguish logs, metrics, and traces by the question each one answers
Explain why averages and dashboards hide the failures that matter
Reason about cardinality, sampling, and what they cost you
Alert on symptoms users feel rather than causes you guessed

exercises.title: Metrics, logs, and traces preserve different dimensions of system behavior
exercises.body: A metric aggregates numeric measurements over time. A log records one event with its fields. A distributed trace links timed spans from one request across services using a propagated trace identifier. Operators combine them to detect a change, inspect an event, and locate latency or failure along a request path.
exercises.note: Each signal covers only instrumented code paths and recorded fields. An uninstrumented failure can occur while every collected series remains healthy.

exercises.prompt: Show the minimum components and flows that implement this mechanism: Metrics, logs, and traces preserve different dimensions of system behavior
exercises.why: A metric aggregates numeric measurements over time. A log records one event with its fields. A distributed trace links timed spans from one request across services using a propagated trace identifier. Operators combine them to detect a change, inspect an event, and locate latency or failure along a request path. Each signal covers only instrumented code paths and recorded fields. An uninstrumented failure can occur while every collected series remains healthy.

exercises.prompt: One checkout crosses three services, but their logs cannot be connected. Propagate one trace ID through every call.
exercises.beforeStatus: INCIDENT SEARCH · thousands of unrelated log lines · slow call unknown
exercises.afterStatus: TRACE · one request path · Inventory span accounts for 2.8 seconds
exercises.why: Propagating trace context links spans from one request across service boundaries and exposes where its time was spent. Sampling and correct context propagation still matter; a missing span can break the path.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: One checkout crosses three services, but their logs cannot be connected. Propagate one trace ID through every call. Place Inventory, Payment. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Checkout API → Inventory; Inventory → Payment. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Propagating trace context links spans from one request across service boundaries and exposes where its time was spent. Sampling and correct context propagation still matter; a missing span can break the path.

exercises.prompt: Your service is slow. Your CPU graph looks fine. What does that actually tell you?
choices: Only that this aggregate CPU graph does not establish CPU as the cause; inspect per-core use, throttling, queues, and wait time before ruling CPU in or out
exercises.why: An average CPU graph can look normal while one core is saturated, a container is throttled, brief peaks are averaged away, or only the affected host is overloaded. Per-core utilization, throttling, run queues, and CPU wait data are needed before excluding CPU; dependency, lock, disk, and network waits remain alternative causes.

exercises.prompt: Match each signal to the question it answers.

pairs.right: Is something wrong, and how much?
What exactly happened in this one case?
Where did the time go across services?

exercises.why: Metrics aggregate measurements across events, logs record details of individual events, and traces connect timed spans from one request across services. Together they support detection with metrics, localization with traces, and event-level diagnosis with logs.

exercises.prompt: Why can't you just log everything and skip metrics?
choices: Logs cost roughly per event, so at high traffic the volume and bill explode — and answering 'what's my error rate?' means scanning them, while a metric already knows
exercises.why: Metrics pre-aggregate observations into bounded time series, while logging every request creates storage and ingestion proportional to traffic. Logs preserve event detail, but metrics provide affordable rates, percentiles, and alerts at high volume, so both signals serve different queries.

exercises.prompt: One distributed trace shows the timed spans below. Tap the span that dominates this request's critical path.
exercises.why: The inventory span consumes 2,740 ms, far more than the other recorded spans, so it dominates the traced request's latency. The trace localizes waiting to that dependency path; inventory's own metrics and logs are then needed to distinguish its internal cause.

exercises.prompt: Build the tracing path so gateway and checkout spans become one end-to-end trace instead of unrelated fragments.
exercises.why: The gateway passes the existing trace and parent identifiers on the checkout call, and both services export their spans to a backend that joins them by those identifiers. If checkout starts a fresh trace instead, its latency and errors remain recorded but cannot be correlated reliably with the originating request path.

exercises.prompt: What's the actual difference between 'monitoring' and 'observability'?
choices: Monitoring answers questions you thought of in advance; observability is having enough signal to answer questions you didn't
Observability is just monitoring with more dashboards
Monitoring is for infrastructure, observability for apps
exercises.why: Monitoring checks predefined conditions, while observability describes whether emitted telemetry supports new questions about internal state. Retaining sufficiently structured metrics, logs, and traces allows an engineer to investigate an unanticipated failure without first adding instrumentation and waiting for it to recur.

exercises.title: Latency percentiles expose slow requests hidden by the mean
exercises.body: Sort request latencies from fastest to slowest. The `p95` value is the latency at or below which 95% of observations fall; the slowest 5% exceed it. A mean compresses the full distribution into one value, so a small group of very slow requests can remain invisible.
exercises.note: Track percentiles by operation and region. Aggregating unrelated workloads can hide a severe tail in a low-volume endpoint or location.

exercises.prompt: Sort 100 request latencies: 95 are 80ms, 4 are 500ms, and 1 is 6,000ms. Using nearest-rank p99, what is p99?
exercises.why: With 100 sorted observations, nearest-rank p99 is the 99th value. Positions 96 through 99 are 500 ms, while only position 100 is 6,000 ms, so p99 is 500 ms. The mean is `(95 × 80 + 4 × 500 + 1 × 6,000) ÷ 100 = 156 ms`; that single average still hides both tail cohorts.

exercises.prompt: Your service returns `200 OK` for every request, including ones where the internal work failed. What did that cost you?
choices: Nothing — the errors are in the logs
Your error rate metric reads 0% during a real outage, so monitoring, alerting, and every retry policy all believe you're healthy
exercises.why: If failed work is reported as `200 OK`, status-derived error metrics count those requests as successes. Alerts, service-level indicators, clients, and caches then operate on incorrect outcome data, so the application must expose failures through an accurate status or an explicit success signal.

exercises.prompt: Which make an incident harder to diagnose? Select all.
choices: Logs without a request id to correlate them
exercises.why: Averages collapse slow tail requests into one aggregate, logs need a shared request ID for cross-component correlation, and false success codes undercount failures. Latency percentiles preserve the distribution boundary at each reported percentile, making slow cohorts visible during diagnosis.

exercises.prompt: What are the four 'golden signals' worth measuring on any service?
choices: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation — how slow, how much, how broken, how full
exercises.why: Latency measures response time, traffic measures demand, errors measure unsuccessful work, and saturation measures how fully a constrained resource is used. These signals cover current user-visible behavior and remaining capacity; host CPU and memory alone can miss limits such as a full connection pool or growing queue.

exercises.prompt: Why is saturation the signal that warns you EARLY?
choices: Because latency and errors only degrade once you're near the limit, while saturation is rising the whole way there — it tells you you're heading for the cliff before you're on it
exercises.why: Saturation measures utilization of a finite resource such as worker slots, connections, or queue capacity. It can rise before user-visible latency because waiting time grows sharply as available capacity approaches zero, making saturation useful for capacity warnings.

exercises.prompt: Your metrics say the service is healthy. Users say it's broken. Who's right?
choices: Neither source settles it alone: reproduce the path and segment telemetry by client, region, operation, and dependency
The users, always, even before reproducing the report
The dashboard, because aggregates cannot be wrong
exercises.why: A report may be client-specific, mistaken, or outside the measured service, while a green aggregate may hide one region or path. Reproduction and segmented telemetry establish scope. Once the failure is confirmed, green metrics reveal an instrumentation gap in the affected user outcome.

exercises.title: Metric label cardinality determines the number of stored time series
exercises.body: A metrics backend creates a separate time series for each distinct combination of metric name and label values. Labels combine multiplicatively: 8 routes × 5 statuses × 4 regions produce 160 series before adding instances or versions.
exercises.note: Unbounded labels such as request identifiers can create millions of series, increasing memory, storage, query latency, and ingestion cost.

exercises.prompt: A latency metric has 12 routes, 5 statuses, 3 regions, and a `user_id` label with 10 million possible values. If every combination occurs, how many time series can it create?
exercises.why: Label dimensions multiply: `12 × 5 × 3 × 10,000,000 = 1,800,000,000` possible series. This cardinality can overwhelm ingestion, indexes, memory, and queries. Store per-user identifiers in event-oriented logs or traces; keep metric labels bounded to dimensions suitable for continuous aggregation.

exercises.prompt: So where does high-cardinality detail like user_id belong?
choices: In logs and traces, which are per-event by nature and priced accordingly — you look them up when investigating rather than aggregating them continuously
exercises.why: Logs and traces store individual events or spans, so a `user_id` can remain a searchable field without creating one persistent metric series per user. Metrics should retain low-cardinality dimensions for aggregation, while traces identify slow requests and logs provide their detailed events.

exercises.prompt: Uniform 1% sampling retains at least one trace from 100 failed requests only about 63% of the time. What operational conclusion follows?
choices: Uniform sampling reliably preserves every incident
Rare failures can disappear from the sampled traces, so error-biased or tail-based sampling is safer for diagnosis
The service should stop collecting metrics
Increasing log retention guarantees the missing traces will appear
exercises.why: Uniform sampling discards each trace independently, so an incident can leave no retained failure trace even when many requests failed. Error-biased or tail-based policies preferentially retain diagnostically valuable traces instead of asking the learner to compute an exponential probability on a phone.

exercises.prompt: Which are real costs of observability? Select all.
choices: Storage and ingest bills that can rival the service's own cost
Instrumentation overhead in the request path
Engineer time maintaining dashboards and alerts nobody reads
exercises.why: Telemetry requires storage and ingestion, instrumentation consumes application resources, and dashboards and alerts require maintenance as services change. Query performance is not inherently reduced by having observability; any overhead depends on how telemetry is collected and exported.

exercises.prompt: A service emits a 2KB event for each of 1 billion daily requests. Ignoring indexes and replicas, how much raw storage does 7 days of full hot retention require? Use decimal units.
exercises.why: `2 KB × 1 billion = 2 TB/day`, so seven days require 14 TB before indexing or replication. Ninety days would require 180 TB. If responders query only seven days but compliance needs 90 days for 0.1% of security events, keep the short full window hot and route that defined subset to cheaper long-term storage.

exercises.prompt: Why are structured logs worth more than free-text ones?
choices: Because they're queryable: 'all errors for user 42 on checkout in the last hour' is a filter over fields, not a regex over prose
exercises.why: Structured logs encode fields such as `request_id`, `status`, and `duration_ms` consistently, allowing reliable filtering, grouping, and aggregation. Free-text logs require parsing variable sentences and can make the same value difficult to query across services.

lessons.title: Telemetry can overload its own pipeline

exercises.title: The telemetry pipeline has its own capacity limit
exercises.body: Logs, metrics, and traces enter ingestion workers before storage. If emission exceeds ingestion, telemetry queues grow precisely when an incident creates more errors. Sampling, admission policy, and spare capacity keep the diagnostic path usable.
exercises.note: Preserve errors and representative traces before repetitive low-value events.

exercises.prompt: Services emit 80,000 events/sec. Each ingestion worker handles 20,000/sec. Over 60 seconds, choose the *fewest* workers that prevent telemetry backlog growth.
exercises.why: Three workers process 60,000 events/sec and accumulate 1.2 million events in one minute. Four match arrivals. Production capacity should exceed that knife edge so bursts and worker failures do not blind the system.

exercises.title: Paging alerts should measure sustained user-visible failure
exercises.body: A page signals that immediate human action is required. Base it on symptoms such as elevated error rate, breached latency objectives, or failed critical transactions over a defined duration. Internal resource saturation is a diagnostic signal unless it reliably predicts imminent user impact.
exercises.note: Noisy cause-based pages produce alert fatigue and slow response to real incidents. Route non-urgent capacity conditions to tickets or dashboards instead.

exercises.prompt: You alert on 'CPU above 80%'. It fires at 2am. The service is serving users perfectly. What did you do wrong?
choices: You alerted on a cause rather than a symptom — high CPU isn't a problem unless users feel it, so you woke someone for a number
exercises.why: CPU above 80% is a resource condition, but the prompt states that service outcomes remain healthy, so it does not justify an urgent page by itself. User-impact alerts should track symptoms such as sustained error rate or latency; CPU saturation can drive a capacity warning or investigation.

exercises.prompt: What's the test for whether something deserves to page a human at 3am?
choices: Whether a human must act NOW to stop users being harmed — if it can wait until morning, it's a ticket, not a page
exercises.why: A pager alert should indicate urgent user impact or an imminent failure that the on-call can mitigate. Non-urgent or non-actionable conditions belong in dashboards or tickets; paging on them raises the false-positive rate and makes critical alerts harder to identify.

exercises.prompt: Which are good pages? Select all.
choices: p99 latency above the SLO for 10 minutes
Disk will be full in 4 hours, cleanup is not automated, and on-call needs 2 hours to prevent exhaustion
exercises.why: Sustained error rates and latency show ongoing user impact. Disk exhaustion in four hours also warrants a page here because no automation will recover it and a human needs two hours to intervene. A single `500 Internal Server Error` is one sample; it should page only when an aggregate rate, duration, or burn-rate threshold indicates material impact.

exercises.prompt: Why do good alerts have a duration — '5% errors for 5 minutes' rather than '5% errors'?
choices: Because a momentary spike is normal and self-correcting: requiring it to persist filters out the noise that would otherwise page you constantly
To give the system time to fix itself
exercises.why: A duration condition distinguishes sustained failure from brief threshold crossings caused by deployment, garbage collection, or a small traffic sample. Requiring the error rate to remain above 5% for a defined interval reduces pages for incidents that resolve before intervention is possible.

exercises.prompt: Checkout and search both fail behind one database incident. Build a paging path that preserves user-impact alerts but sends one actionable notification.
exercises.why: Sustained user-impact rules turn checkout and search failures into meaningful alerts, then dependency-aware grouping correlates both symptoms to one database incident before paging. Without grouping, one dependency failure can create a page storm; suppressing symptom alerts instead can hide the user impact that makes the incident urgent.

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: Checkout and search both fail behind one database incident. Build a paging path that preserves user-impact alerts but sends one actionable notification.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Checkout errors → User-impact Alert Rules; Search errors → User-impact Alert Rules; User-impact Alert Rules → Dependency-aware incident grouping; Dependency-aware incident grouping → Pager. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Sustained user-impact rules turn checkout and search failures into meaningful alerts, then dependency-aware grouping correlates both symptoms to one database incident before paging. Without grouping, one dependency failure can create a page storm; suppressing symptom alerts instead can hide the user impact that makes the incident urgent.

exercises.prompt: What's the honest summary of observability?
choices: More dashboards and more alerts mean more reliability

It's the ability to answer questions you didn't anticipate — metrics to know something's wrong, traces to find where, logs to see what — bought with real money and real engineer time, and ruined by dishonest signals and noisy alerts
It's a monitoring tool you install
exercises.why: Observability depends on telemetry that accurately represents system behavior: metrics expose aggregate outcomes, logs preserve event details, and traces connect request paths. Missing instrumentation and misleading signals such as false success codes or averages without tail percentiles prevent reliable diagnosis.

exercises.prompt: A checkout request crosses six services. Metrics show elevated latency but not which hop consumed it. What evidence connects the slow spans for this one request?
choices: A distributed trace carrying one trace context
One log file with no request identifier
exercises.why: Trace context links spans across service boundaries and exposes the critical path for one request. Metrics reveal the population-level symptom but not that request's hop-by-hop timing.
